newsitem.title: UK: UK Conservatives crumple into recrimination.
newsitem.headline: UK Conservatives crumple into recrimination.

text.p: Britain's Conservative Party crumpled into recrimination on Friday after suffering an electoral defeat more crushing than ministers ever believed possible.

With five ministers in John Major's cabinet losing their seats as the Labour Party charged towards the biggest landslide for more than 150 years, Conservatives scrambled to find scapegoats for their humiliation.
Candidates for an expected battle to succeed Major as party leader held back from overt criticism of the prime minister and called for a period of calm consideration.
At least two leadership candidates, Michael Portillo and Malcolm Rifkind, lost their seats and are thus ruled out of any contest.
But before half the results were in, a group representing the left of the Conservative Party issued a statement accusing the party's right wing of treachery.
"The election defeat that the Conservative party experienced was wholly unnnecessary. It was brought about by the rank treachery of the Tory (Conservative) right.

"They, ably assisted by the newpapers that backed them, have run a vile campaign of hatred against John Major and his administration almost from the moment of the sensational victory of 1992," the Tory Reform group said.

Major snatched an election victory against the odds in 1992 but right-wing Eurosceptics have made his life hell since then by demanding that he rule out joining a single European currency and halt closer links with Brussels.

The Tory Reform Group's outburst was met in kind by one of the Eurosceptics they sought to vilify, Nicholas Winterton. He blamed finance minister Kenneth Clarke for losing the election because of his soft line on Europe.
"He will be remembered, even reviled in history for his actions," Winterton said.
Party maverick Edwina Currie decried the six-week campaign battle against a rejuvenated Labour Party as "a shambles".
"Obviously any party that gives the impression of not being united, that cannot help you in an election," said Foreign Secretary Rifkind.

Former party chairman Norman Tebbit, a right-winger close to former premier Margaret Thatcher, was quick to blame Major for not taking into account the strength of opposition within his party to closer links with Europe.
"If he (Major) had led that change of view in the party, the view of the great mass of the people, he would have stood a very good chance of winning the election," Tebbit said.

Analysts said that the Conservatives' defeat was certain to lead to calls for Major's resignation. Portillo had been expected to be the Eurosceptics' favoured candidate to succeed him as party leader.
Portillo said a battle to unite the party lay ahead.

"The party was pretty divided...and for the first time I can speak without anyone suspecting me of leadership ambitions, I can now say I plead with the party not to fall into disunity and opposition because that would be the way of staying there."

Major's deputy Michael Heseltine, who himself stood as a leadership candidate against Margaret Thatcher in 1990, called for a "mature period of reflection" and said he would back Major in any contest.
